formulas.name: Pythagoras' theorem

variables.name: hypotenuse
variables.description: The longest side, opposite the right angle.

variables.name: first leg
variables.description: One of the two shorter sides.

variables.name: second leg
variables.description: The other shorter side.

formulas.explanation: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. One proof: four copies of the triangle fit inside a square of side a + b, leaving a tilted square of side c in the middle. Comparing areas gives (a + b)² = 4 × ½ab + c², which simplifies to c² = a² + b².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever a right angle is involved and you know two sides: ladders, diagonals, distances on a map, screen sizes.
assumptions: the triangle has a right angle between a and b

example.story: A 5 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 1.5 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?

formulas.name: Sine in a right-angled triangle (SOH)

variables.name: angle
variables.description: One of the acute angles, in radians.

variables.name: opposite side
variables.description: The side facing the angle θ.

variables.name: hypotenuse
variables.description: The longest side, opposite the right angle.

formulas.explanation: All right-angled triangles with the same angle θ are scaled copies of each other, so the ratio opposite over hypotenuse depends only on θ. That ratio is called the sine of θ. SOH CAH TOA is the usual way to remember which ratio is which.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when the problem involves the side opposite an angle and the hypotenuse, such as the height reached by a ramp or a kite string.
assumptions: θ in radians (multiply degrees by π/180)

example.story: A ramp 4 m long rises at 30 degrees (π/6 rad) to the ground. How high does it climb?

formulas.name: Cosine in a right-angled triangle (CAH)

variables.name: angle
variables.description: One of the acute angles, in radians.

variables.name: adjacent side
variables.description: The side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse.

variables.name: hypotenuse
variables.description: The longest side, opposite the right angle.

formulas.explanation: The cosine of an angle is the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse. Like the sine, it depends only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle. To find an angle from two sides, use the inverse function acos (cos⁻¹).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when the problem involves the side next to an angle and the hypotenuse, for example the horizontal distance covered by a slope.

example.story: A 6 m rope is tied to the top of a pole and pegged to the ground 3 m from its base. What angle does the rope make with the ground?

formulas.name: Tangent in a right-angled triangle (TOA)

variables.name: angle
variables.description: One of the acute angles, in radians.

variables.name: opposite side
variables.description: The side facing the angle θ.

variables.name: adjacent side
variables.description: The side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse.

formulas.explanation: The tangent is the ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent side, so it does not need the hypotenuse at all. It is also the gradient of a line at angle θ to the horizontal. This makes it ideal for heights measured from a distance.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for angles of elevation and depression, slopes and gradients, whenever the hypotenuse is not involved.

example.story: Standing 20 m from a tree, you look up to its top at an angle of 35 degrees (0.6109 rad). How tall is the tree above your eye level?

formulas.name: Angle sum of a triangle

variables.name: first angle
variables.description: One interior angle, in degrees.

variables.name: second angle
variables.description: Another interior angle, in degrees.

variables.name: third angle
variables.description: The remaining interior angle, in degrees.

formulas.explanation: Draw a line through one corner parallel to the opposite side. The two alternate angles it makes equal the other two angles of the triangle, and together with the third angle they form a straight line, 180 degrees. In radians the sum is π.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the third angle of a triangle before applying the sine or cosine rule.
assumptions: flat (Euclidean) geometry; on a sphere the sum is larger

example.story: Two angles of a triangle are 50 and 60 degrees. What is the third?

formulas.name: Sine rule

variables.name: side a
variables.description: The side opposite angle α.

variables.name: angle α
variables.description: The angle opposite side a, in radians.

variables.name: side b
variables.description: The side opposite angle β.

variables.name: angle β
variables.description: The angle opposite side b, in radians.

formulas.explanation: In any triangle, each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same number (the diameter of the circumscribed circle). Drop a perpendicular height h: it equals b sin α and also a sin β, and setting them equal gives the rule. When finding an angle, beware the ambiguous case: an obtuse angle with the same sine may also fit.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for a triangle without a right angle when you know a side and its opposite angle plus one more side or angle.
assumptions: the ambiguous case can give two triangles when solving for an angle

example.story: In a triangle, side a = 10 m is opposite a 45 degree angle. How long is side b, opposite a 60 degree angle?
steps: b = a sin β / sin α

formulas.name: Cosine rule

variables.name: side c
variables.description: The side opposite angle γ.

variables.name: side a
variables.description: One side next to γ.

variables.name: side b
variables.description: The other side next to γ.

variables.name: angle γ
variables.description: The angle between sides a and b, in radians.

formulas.explanation: The cosine rule is Pythagoras' theorem with a correction for angles that are not 90 degrees. When γ is a right angle, cos γ = 0 and it becomes c² = a² + b². An obtuse angle has a negative cosine, which makes c longer, as you would expect.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when you know two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides (solve for the angle).

example.story: Two straight paths of 7 m and 9 m leave a point at 60 degrees to each other. How far apart are their ends?

formulas.name: Area of a triangle from two sides and the included angle

variables.name: area
variables.description: Area of the triangle.

variables.name: side a
variables.description: One side.

variables.name: side b
variables.description: Another side.

variables.name: included angle
variables.description: The angle between sides a and b, in radians.

formulas.explanation: Take side a as the base. The perpendicular height from the opposite corner is b sin γ, so ½ × base × height becomes ½ab sin γ. The angle must be the one between the two known sides.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when you know two sides and the angle between them but not the height.
assumptions: γ is the angle between a and b

example.story: A triangular plot has sides of 8 m and 11 m with a 30 degree angle between them. What is its area?

formulas.name: Pythagorean identity

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Any angle, in radians.

formulas.explanation: On the unit circle, the point at angle θ has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ). Its distance from the origin is 1, so by Pythagoras cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 for every angle. Dividing by cos²θ gives the related identity 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find cos θ from sin θ (or the other way round), and to simplify trigonometric expressions.

example.story: Check the identity for θ = 0.7 rad.

formulas.name: Tangent as sine over cosine

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Any angle where cos θ is not zero, in radians.

formulas.explanation: In a right-angled triangle, opposite/adjacent equals (opposite/hypotenuse) divided by (adjacent/hypotenuse), which is sin θ / cos θ. This definition works for every angle, and shows that tan θ is undefined where cos θ = 0, at 90 degrees, 270 degrees and so on.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to rewrite tan in terms of sin and cos when simplifying or solving equations.

example.story: Check the identity for θ = 1 rad.

formulas.name: Double angle formula for sine

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Any angle, in radians.

formulas.explanation: Put β = α = θ in the compound angle formula sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β. The two terms are equal, giving 2 sin θ cos θ.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to simplify products sin θ cos θ, to solve equations like sin 2x = sin x, and in projectile range calculations.

example.story: Check the identity for θ = 0.5 rad.

formulas.name: Double angle formula for cosine

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Any angle, in radians.

formulas.explanation: Put α = β = θ in cos(α + β) = cos α cos β - sin α sin β. Using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 you can write the result in two more forms, 2cos²θ - 1 and 1 - 2sin²θ, which are handy for integrating sin² and cos².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to remove squares of sine or cosine, and to solve equations mixing cos 2x with sin x or cos x.

example.story: Check the identity for θ = 0.5 rad.

formulas.name: Double angle formula for tangent

variables.name: angle
variables.description: An angle where both sides are defined, in radians.

formulas.explanation: Divide sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ by cos 2θ = cos²θ - sin²θ, then divide the top and bottom by cos²θ. Each sin/cos becomes a tan.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to simplify or solve equations involving tan 2x when tan x is known.

example.story: Check the identity for θ = 0.3 rad.

formulas.name: Sine of a sum of angles

variables.name: first angle
variables.description: Any angle, in radians.

variables.name: second angle
variables.description: Any angle, in radians. Replace β by -β for sin(α - β).

formulas.explanation: The sine of a sum is not the sum of the sines. This addition formula can be proved by rotating a point on the unit circle twice, or from the area of a triangle split into two right-angled pieces. Replacing β by -β gives sin(α - β) = sin α cos β - cos α sin β.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find exact values like sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°), and to combine a sin x + b cos x into a single wave.

example.story: Check the formula for α = 0.5 rad and β = 0.3 rad.

formulas.name: Cosine of a sum of angles

variables.name: first angle
variables.description: Any angle, in radians.

variables.name: second angle
variables.description: Any angle, in radians. Replace β by -β for cos(α - β).

formulas.explanation: The cosine of a sum combines the products of cosines and sines with a minus sign. For a difference the sign flips: cos(α - β) = cos α cos β + sin α sin β. Setting α = β gives the double angle formula for cosine.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for exact values like cos 15° = cos(45° - 30°), and when expanding or simplifying trigonometric expressions.

example.story: Check the formula for α = 0.5 rad and β = 0.3 rad.

formulas.name: Tangent of a sum of angles

variables.name: first angle
variables.description: An angle in radians where tan is defined.

variables.name: second angle
variables.description: An angle in radians where tan is defined.

formulas.explanation: Divide the sine sum formula by the cosine sum formula and then divide every term by cos α cos β. It is useful for the angle between two lines, because each line's gradient is the tangent of its angle.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to add angles given by their tangents, such as the angle between two lines with known gradients.

example.story: Check the formula for α = 0.5 rad and β = 0.3 rad.

formulas.name: Power reduction formula for sine squared

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Any angle, in radians.

formulas.explanation: Rearranging cos 2θ = 1 - 2 sin²θ expresses a square of sine as a plain cosine of the double angle. The same trick gives cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2. These forms are what you need to integrate sin² and cos².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to integrate sin²x, to find the average of sin² over a cycle (it is ½), or in AC power calculations.

example.story: Check the identity for θ = 0.4 rad.

formulas.name: Degrees to radians

variables.name: angle in radians
variables.description: The angle measured in radians.

variables.name: angle in degrees
variables.description: The angle measured in degrees.

formulas.explanation: A full turn is 360 degrees or 2π radians, so 180 degrees equals π radians. Multiply by π/180 to go from degrees to radians and by 180/π to go back. One radian is about 57.3 degrees.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it before applying formulas that need radians, such as arc length, angular velocity and calculus with trig functions.

example.story: Convert 135 degrees to radians.

formulas.name: Polar to Cartesian (x coordinate)

variables.name: x coordinate
variables.description: Horizontal position.

variables.name: distance from origin
variables.description: The polar radius.

variables.name: polar angle
variables.description: Angle measured anticlockwise from the positive x axis.

formulas.explanation: A point at distance r and angle θ from the origin forms a right-angled triangle with the x axis. The horizontal side of that triangle is r cos θ. The same idea splits forces and velocities into horizontal components.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to convert polar coordinates to Cartesian ones, or to find the horizontal component of a vector.
assumptions: angle in radians measured from the positive x axis

example.story: A point lies 4 m from the origin at an angle of 30 degrees (π/6). What is its x coordinate?

formulas.name: Polar to Cartesian (y coordinate)

variables.name: y coordinate
variables.description: Vertical position.

variables.name: distance from origin
variables.description: The polar radius.

variables.name: polar angle
variables.description: Angle measured anticlockwise from the positive x axis.

formulas.explanation: The vertical side of the triangle formed by the point, the origin and the x axis is r sin θ. Together with x = r cos θ this converts polar coordinates to Cartesian, and by Pythagoras x² + y² = r².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to convert polar coordinates, or to find the vertical component of a force or velocity.
assumptions: angle in radians measured from the positive x axis

example.story: A point lies 4 m from the origin at an angle of 30 degrees (π/6). What is its y coordinate?
